Disease Outbreak Disrupts Sri Lankan Transportation and Logistics Sector

A sudden outbreak of leptospirosis has struck Sri Lanka’s transportation and logistics industry, leading to severe workforce shortages and delays at several key logistics hubs. The disease, commonly known as rat fever and often contracted through water contaminated by animal urine, was first reported last week among workers at the Colombo Inland Freight Terminal. Since then, infections have been confirmed at three additional sites in the Western and Southern provinces.

Health officials estimate that over 230 logistics workers have tested positive for leptospirosis to date, with more than 600 currently under observation. The outbreak has forced several operators, including TransAsia Freightlines and Lankaport Logistics, to scale back operations or temporarily close affected warehouses for deep cleaning and disinfection.

“We are facing an unprecedented situation,” said M. Karunaratne, president of the National Freight Association of Sri Lanka. “Our members are experiencing absenteeism rates of up to 40 percent in some facilities, and the movement of goods has slowed considerably.”

The Sri Lanka Ports Authority confirmed that cargo processing times at the Colombo port have increased by 36 percent in the past week. Exporters and importers are reporting shipment backlogs and container delays, as the available workforce struggles to maintain normal throughput.

According to the Sri Lankan Hauliers’ Union, at least 120 truck drivers have been hospitalized since the outbreak began. “We’re seeing a shortage of drivers for both long-haul and last-mile deliveries,” said union secretary S. Jayasinghe. “With the monsoon rains worsening flooding in some areas, the risk of further transmission is high.”

The Ministry of Health has deployed mobile clinics to major logistics sites and initiated a vaccination campaign targeting high-risk workers. However, Dr. N. Weerasinghe, an epidemiologist advising the response, cautioned that containment could take weeks. “Leptospirosis is difficult to control in the current weather conditions. We urge companies to reinforce hygiene measures and provide protective gear.”

Industry analysts say the outbreak is likely to impact supply chains both domestically and for regional transshipment. “If the situation persists, costs will rise and delivery schedules will slip further,” said Ayesha Perera, a logistics sector consultant based in Colombo.

As authorities work to contain the outbreak, transportation and logistics operators are bracing for ongoing disruptions and the potential for wider economic repercussions within the sector.
